source.title: Not All Refusals Are Equal: How Safety Alignment Fails Cybersecurity at Scale
source.authors: Vadym Hadetskyi; Dario Pasquini; A.E. Sorokin

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies the harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference direction and orthogonal weight projection, then measures refusal and capability on new models and domain-specific settings. It changes the extraction prompts and layer coverage from the original setup.
record.gate_note: The paper measures the last-token, per-layer mean-difference direction and removes it from selected down_proj and o_proj weights; it does not add the direction. Extraction details used to select the method are not recorded as result rows. Results cited from other work are not rows. Figure 1 and several figures report per-model values, but the flattened presentation and the 60-row limit prevent recording the full model-by-domain matrix.
record.test_reason: Applies the harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference direction as a permanent weight projection to 24 open models, using domain-specific prompts and 25-95% layer spreads. It reports refusal rates, MMLU, per-domain direction cosines and susceptibility by safety-training method, so it bears on V1, V2, V4 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but the record adds 'consistent with multidimensional representations'. The authors state their results 'corroborate' prior findings of multi-dimensional refusal and extend them with two points: refusal is distributed across layers and experts at trillion scale, and domain-tuned extraction isolates a domain slice. They name safety-training type and architecture as the most reliable predictors of susceptibility and say size is not.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-harmless last-token mean differences and orthogonal projection of weights, but builds domain-specific extraction prompts and modifies selected layers (5–30% across 25–95% of depth), rather than testing the original broad refusal direction across all layers and positions. It does not add the direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by model, domain, evaluation dataset, layer-selection strategy, and abliteration intensity. Uniformly spread layer selection can outperform norm-based selection; the paper reports that the cross-evaluation and scientific datasets yield different effect sizes. Refusal reduction also varies across reported training methods and architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Cybersecurity-extracted direction yields domain-selective refusal removal in a few models; many models collapse across all domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A domain-specific harmful-minus-harmless direction can be abliterated selectively in some models.

record.code_released: The code, evaluation framework and datasets will be released upon publication.
record.problems: The paper uses 31 string-matching refusal patterns rather than human annotation or an LLM judge; it notes possible missed or misclassified refusals. Evaluation is English-only and cybersecurity-focused. Only one intervention family is tested, only up to 30% of layers is systematically explored, and results depend on the prompt/domain definition. Training-method comparisons are observational. Uncertainty is not stated for most individual Table 2 results.
record.rows_left_out: The full per-model, per-domain results in Figure 1 and dose-response curves in Figure 4 were not transcribed because the figure presentation is flattened and a complete model-by-domain record would exceed the 60-row limit. Figure 5's model-by-model susceptibility values and Figure 7's full layer-selection comparisons are likewise omitted; resistant outcomes explicitly described in the text are retained in r21–r22. Figure 8/9 matrix entries not needed to show the reported domain distinctions are omitted.

untested.parts: No direction addition to induce refusal; no ablation of the direction at every layer and position; capability only via MMLU.
No release or test of a public abliteration tool or its released weights.
No direct test of affine, cone or multi-dimensional subspace structure; only per-domain direction cosines and selective ablation.
No controlled manipulation of how or when refusal is trained.
Not tested; <think> blocks are only stripped for matching.

missing.what: Per-model, per-domain refusal values and dose-response curves; MMLU scores for each model
Layer-selection comparison (uniform vs norm-based, about 70pp gap)
Claim that narrow middle-layer abliteration does not suffice, since refusal is distributed widely across layers and experts in many models
Architecture result: MoE models are more resistant on average than dense models
Stated finding that the refusal-compliance effect is distribution-specific and over-fits to the extraction prompts

record.verdict_notes: The study is a T3 setting: a domain-specific direction and layer-spread edit, not a replication of the original broad direction. The Mistral-Large and GLM-4.7 resistance results therefore challenge V1 and V2 only for this procedure. The authors themselves note that Heretic abliterates such models. The V4 verdict rests on cosine similarities and selectivity, not on a test of cone or subspace structure. The refusal measure is 31 string patterns. Uncertainty is mostly not reported, the text and figures disagree in places (e.g. Kimi K2 22.8pp susceptibility vs 37pp, and the cybersecurity cosine range), and the text calls Kimi K2 high-susceptibility but Table 3 labels GLM-4.7 partial.

versions.untested_parts: No direction addition or harmless-request refusal induction; projection is applied to selected layers (5–30% across 25–95% of model depth), not every layer and position. Capability is assessed with MMLU, not a broad ability suite.
Tests the paper's own permanent weight edits, but does not report release of its modified model weights or test a separately released abliteration tool.
Does not test whether jailbreak attacks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation improves robustness.
Measures domain-specific direction similarities and selective ablation, but does not directly test affine or cone models of refusal geometry.
Does not separate a harmfulness judgment from a refusal decision.
Does not test transfer of a direction across languages, base/instruct stages, or model variants.
Compares susceptibility across models with different reported safety-training methods; it does not manipulate training method or timing under controlled conditions.
Does not test whether the claim holds in reasoning models; stripping <think> blocks for refusal matching is not a reasoning-model comparison.

source_check.notes: The record's code=y is wrong: code and datasets 'will be released upon the publication'. Uncertainty is only the SD across models (Fig 2), and refusal is scored by 31 string patterns. The paper contradicts itself in several places: GLM-4.7 is 'fully resistant' in Sec 4 but Partial in Table 3/Fig 5; the cosine range in the prose (0.56-0.70) differs from Fig 9 (0.62-0.75); the five models span 3.8B per the text but the named ones start at 8.2B; Kimi K2 is 22.8pp in Sec 5.1 but -37pp in Table 2(b).
